title: HTTP/HTTPS Under the Microscope
description: Understanding methods, status codes, and user-agents.

slides.title: HTTP: The Web's Building Block 🌐
slides.content:
# Hypertext Transfer Protocol

**HTTP** is a **stateless** request-response protocol. Your browser sends a **Request**, the server sends a **Response**.

**HTTP Request Methods:**
*   **GET:** *"Show me the page."* (Most common)
*   **POST:** *"Here is my login/password or file upload."* (Data submission)
*   **HEAD:** *"Tell me about the page, but don't send it."*
*   **PUT/DELETE:** Used in REST APIs.

**Why Analysts Care:**
*   An unusual **POST** request to a foreign IP from a Finance user? That's **Data Exfiltration**.
*   A **GET** request with an extremely long URL full of weird characters? That's **SQL Injection** or **Buffer Overflow**.

slides.title: Sample HTTP Request (Raw)
slides.content: This is what travels over the wire on Port 80.
slides.codeSnippet:
GET /login.php HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64)
Accept: text/html,application/xhtml+xml
Accept-Language: en-US,en;q=0.9
Connection: keep-alive

quizData.question: You see a log entry: `POST /upload.php HTTP/1.1` from an internal IP to an unknown external IP. The request body is 15MB. What is concerning?

options.text: The user is watching a YouTube video.
A large file is being uploaded (Potential Data Exfiltration).
The user is just loading a webpage.

quizData.explanation: POST with a large body size indicates data being sent *from* the user to the server. If the server is external and unknown, this is a data exfiltration red flag.

slides.title: HTTP Response Status Codes 🚦
slides.content:
# The Server's Answer

You'll see these codes in proxy logs. Knowing them helps you spot failures and malicious redirects.

*   **1xx:** Informational.
*   **2xx:** Success. *(200 OK - Everything worked)*
*   **3xx:** Redirection. *(302 Found - Go here instead)*
*   **4xx:** Client Error. *(403 Forbidden - You can't see this; 404 Not Found - Page doesn't exist)*
*   **5xx:** Server Error. *(500 Internal Server Error - The website is broken)*

**Security Insight:** If you see a **302 Redirect** sending users from `yourbank.com` to `y0urbank.com`, that's a **Phishing attack** in progress.

slides.title: The User-Agent String 🕵️
slides.content:
# Who Is Knocking?

Every HTTP request includes a **User-Agent** header that identifies the browser and operating system.

*   **Normal User:** `Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36`
*   **Python Script (Attack Tool):** `python-requests/2.28.1`
*   **Curl (Command Line Tool):** `curl/7.68.0`

**Detection:** If you see a **User-Agent** string like `Mozilla/4.0 (compatible; MSIE 6.0; Windows NT 5.1)` in 2026... that's **not** a real old computer. That's a **penetration testing tool** (like Metasploit payload) using a **fake/default User-Agent** to blend in.

slides.title: HTTPS: The Encryption Curtain 🧱
slides.content:
## The Analyst's Blind Spot

**HTTPS** adds **TLS/SSL Encryption** on top of HTTP (Port 443).

*   **Good News:** Attackers can't see your passwords or bank details in transit.
*   **Bad News:** **Neither can you.**

If an attacker uses HTTPS to exfiltrate data to `evil.com` on port 443, your firewall logs **ONLY** show:
*   `Source IP: 10.0.0.5 -> Dest IP: 185.142.53.21 : Port 443`

You **cannot** see the URL (`/stolen-data`) or the file being uploaded.

**The Solution:** **SSL/TLS Decryption (SSL Intercept)**. Corporate proxies terminate the HTTPS connection, inspect the content, and re-encrypt it. This is why you install a company certificate on your work laptop. **Without it, the SOC is blind.**
